en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 99, the Subha Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, was staying at Sāvatthī in the residence of a certain householder on some business.
Then the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, said this to the householder in whose residence he was staying:
“I have heard this, householder:
‘Sāvatthī is not devoid of arahants.
Which ascetic or brahmin, then, should we attend upon today?”
“Venerable sir, this Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Venerable sir, please go to visit that Blessed One.
Then the brahmin student Subha, Todeyya’s son, having assented to that householder, approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, the brahmins say this:
‘A householder can succeed in the method, the Dhamma, and the wholesome, but one who has gone forth cannot succeed in the method, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.’”
“What does Master Gotama say about this?
“In this matter, young man, I am one who speaks analytically;
I do not speak categorically.”
“Student, I do not praise wrong practice for either a householder or one who has gone forth.
For whether it be a householder or one who has gone forth, student, one who practices wrongly does not, on account of that wrong practice, achieve the true way, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.
Student, I do praise right practice for either a householder or one who has gone forth.”
“Whether a householder, young man, or one gone forth, one who practices rightly is successful because of that right practice in attaining the method, the Dhamma, and what is wholesome.
“Master Gotama, the brahmins say this:
‘The work of the household life is a great matter, a great task, a great undertaking, and a great exertion; it is of great fruit.’”
“‘The going forth as a recluse is a task of little substance, of little duty, of little legal dispute, of little exertion, and it yields little fruit.
What does Master Gotama say about this?
“In this matter too, young man, I am one who speaks with analysis.”
I do not take a one-sided position on this matter.
There is, young man, a field of action that is of great purpose, great duty, great consequence, and great undertaking, which, when it fails, yields little fruit;
and there is, young man, a field of action that is of great purpose, great duty, great consequence, and great undertaking, which, when it succeeds, yields great fruit.
“There is, young man, a subject of meditation that has little purpose, little duty, little legal consequence, and little exertion, yet when it fails, it yields little fruit.
There is, young man, a subject of meditation that has little purpose, little duty, little legal consequence, and little exertion, yet when it succeeds, it yields great fruit.
And what, young man, is the subject of meditation that has great purpose, great duty, great legal consequence, and great exertion, yet when it fails, it yields little fruit?”
Agriculture, young man, is a task of great purpose, great duty, great responsibility, and great exertion; when it fails, it yields little fruit.
And what, young man, is the task of great purpose, great duty, great responsibility, and great exertion that, when successful, yields great fruit?
Agriculture itself, young man, is the task of great purpose, great duty, great responsibility, and great exertion that, when successful, yields great fruit.
And what, young man, is that field of action which, when failing, has little purpose, little work, little legal consequence, little exertion, and yields little fruit?
Trade, young man, is a field of action which, when failing, has little purpose, little work, little legal consequence, little exertion, and yields little fruit.
And what, young man, is that field of action which, when succeeding, has little purpose, little work, little legal consequence, little exertion, and yields great fruit?
“Trade, young man, is indeed a task that, when successful, yields great fruit— requiring little effort, little work, little administration, and little exertion. Just as farming,
young man, is a task that, when it fails, yields little fruit— requiring much effort, much work, much administration,
and much exertion— even so, young man, the household life is a task that, when it fails, yields little fruit— requiring much effort, much work, much administration, and much exertion.”
"Just as, young man, the work of farming, when successful—being of great purpose, great duty, great concern, and great exertion—is of great fruit;
even so, young man, the work of the household life, when successful—being of great purpose, great duty, great concern, and great exertion—is of great fruit.
Just as, young man, the work of trade, when unsuccessful—being of little purpose, little duty, little concern, and little exertion—is of little fruit..."
“In the same way, young man, the going-forth as a monk is a task that requires little effort, little work, little administration, and little exertion; yet when it fails, it yields little fruit.
Just as trade itself is a task that requires little effort, little work, little administration, and little exertion, but when successful, yields great fruit;
even so, young man, the going-forth as a monk is a task that requires little effort, little work, little administration, and little exertion, but when successful, yields great fruit.”
“Master Gotama, the brahmins prescribe five things for the performance of merit and for the attainment of the wholesome.
“Māṇava, if it is not troublesome to you, [please explain] those five things which the brahmins prescribe for the performance of merit and for the attainment of the wholesome.”
“It would be well for you to speak on these five qualities in this assembly.
“Venerable Gotama, it is not a burden for me to speak where the Blessed One himself, or one like the Blessed One, is seated.
“In that case, young man, speak.”
“Venerable Gotama, it is true that brahmins prescribe truth as the first principle for the performance of merit and the attainment of the wholesome.
Venerable Gotama, it is true that brahmins prescribe austerity as the second principle for the performance of merit and the attainment of the wholesome.
Venerable Gotama, it is true that brahmins prescribe the holy life as the third principle for the performance of merit and the attainment of the wholesome.”
"Furthermore, Master Gotama, the brahmins prescribe study as the fourth quality for the performance of merit and the attainment of the wholesome.
Furthermore, Master Gotama, the brahmins prescribe generosity as the fifth quality for the performance of merit and the attainment of the wholesome.
Thus, Master Gotama, these five qualities the brahmins prescribe for the performance of merit and the attainment of the wholesome."
“What does Master Gotama say about this?
“But, young man, is there even a single brahmin among the brahmins who says:
‘Having realized these five qualities for myself through direct higher knowledge, I proclaim their result’?”
“No, Master Gotama.
“But, young man, is there even a single teacher among the brahmins, or a teacher’s teacher, or even one who goes back as far as the seventh generation of teachers, who has said this:
‘Having realized these five things for myself through direct higher knowledge, I proclaim their result’?”
“No, Master Gotama.

“But what do you think, young man? Even those ancient seers of the brahmins—the makers of the hymns, the proclaimers of the hymns, whose ancient verses of hymns are now chanted, proclaimed, and rehearsed by the brahmins today—did they not all say this?”
They repeat what has been spoken and recite what has been chanted, namely:
Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu;
they too have said this:
‘Having realized these five qualities for ourselves through direct higher knowledge, we proclaim their result’?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
“In that case, young man, it seems there is not even a single brahmin among the brahmins who says this:”
‘I have realized these five qualities for myself through direct higher knowledge and I proclaim their result’—
not even a single teacher among the brahmins, nor a teacher’s teacher, nor even back to the seventh generation of teachers, has ever said:
‘I have realized these five qualities for myself through direct higher knowledge and I proclaim their result.’
There were also those ancient seers of the brahmins, the makers of the mantras, the proclaimers of the mantras,
whose ancient mantra-words— chanted, proclaimed, and compiled— are still chanted today by the brahmins,
repeated after them, spoken after what was spoken, and taught after what was taught; namely, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, and Vessāmitta.
Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu—
none of them said:
"Having realized for ourselves through direct higher knowledge the ripening of these five qualities, we proclaim them."

"Just as, young man, a line of blind people clinging to one another—the one in front does not see, the one in the middle does not see, and the one in the back does not see—even so, young man, the speech of the brahmins turns out to be like a line of blind people: the one in front does not see, the one in the middle does not see, and the one in the back does not see."

When this was said, the young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, being addressed by the Blessed One with the simile of the blind men, became angry and displeased. Reviling the Blessed One, disparaging the Blessed One, and speaking against the Blessed One, he said, “The ascetic Gotama will be proven wrong,” and addressed the Blessed One thus:
“Master Gotama, the brahmin Pokkharasāti of Opamañña, a follower of Subhaga, says this:”
“In the same way, some recluses and brahmins here claim to possess a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
But their speech turns out to be merely laughable, merely nominal, merely empty, and merely vain.
For how could one who is merely human know, see, or realize a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?”
“Is it not possible for this to happen?
“But what do you think, young man: does the brahmin Pokkharasāti, Opamañño, the son of Subhaga, encompass the minds of all ascetics and brahmins with his own mind and understand them?
“For even his own slave-girl, Puṇṇikā, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, Opamañño, the son of Subhaga—”
“...he does not understand another’s mind by encompassing it with his own mind; how then could he understand the minds of all recluses and brahmins by encompassing them with his own mind?
“It is just as if, young man, a man born blind were unable to see black or white forms, nor could he see...”
He would not see blue forms; he would not see yellow forms; he would not see red forms; he would not see magenta forms;
he would not see even or uneven ground; he would not see the forms of stars; he would not see the moon and sun. He would speak thus:
‘There are no dark or bright forms, nor is there anyone who sees dark or bright forms;
there are no blue forms, nor is there anyone who sees blue forms;
there are no yellow forms, nor is there anyone who sees yellow forms.’
There are no red forms, nor is there anyone who sees red forms;
there are no crimson forms, nor is there anyone who sees crimson forms;
there is neither evenness nor unevenness, nor is there anyone who sees evenness or unevenness.
There are no star-forms, nor anyone who sees star-forms;
there are no moons or suns, nor anyone who sees moons or suns.
I do not know this; I do not see this.
"Therefore, it does not exist.
"Would he, young man, be speaking correctly if he were to say that?
"Certainly not, Master Gotama."
There are black and white forms; there is one who sees black and white forms.
There are blue forms; there is one who sees blue forms.
There are yellow forms; there is one who sees yellow forms.
There are red forms, and there is one who sees red forms;
there are crimson forms, and there is one who sees crimson forms;
there is the level and the uneven, and there is one who sees the level and the uneven.
There are the forms of the stars, and there is one who sees the forms of the stars;
there are the moon and the sun, and there is one who sees the moon and the sun.
‘I do not know this; I do not see this.’
"Therefore, he would not be speaking rightly if he were to say, 'That does not exist,' Master Gotama.
"In the same way, young man, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, the son of Opamañña, is blind and sightless."
"It is impossible that he will know, see, or realize anything further than the human condition—a distinction in noble knowledge and vision.
What do you think, student?
As for those great brahmin householders of Kosala, such as—"

“Caṅkī the brahmin, Tārukkha the brahmin, Pokkharasāti the brahmin, Jāṇussoṇi the brahmin, and your father Todeyya—of these, which is better: that they should speak words that are coherent or words that are incoherent?
“Coherent, Master Gotama.
“Of these, which is better: that they should speak words that are meaningful or words that are meaningless?”
“Is it through wisdom, Master Gotama?
“Of these two, which is better: that they should speak after reflecting, or that they should speak without reflecting?
“That they should speak after reflecting, Master Gotama.”
“Which of these would be better for them: that they should speak words connected with the goal, or words not connected with the goal?
“Words connected with the goal, Master Gotama.
“What do you think, young man?”
“If this is so, was the speech uttered by the brahmin Pokkharasāti of Opamañña at Subhagavana coherent or incoherent?
“It was incoherent, Master Gotama.
“Was the speech uttered as a mantra or not as a mantra?”
“Yes, Master Gotama.
“Is speech spoken after reflection, or without reflection?
“Without reflection, Master Gotama.”
“Is speech that is connected with the goal, or is it speech not connected with the goal?
“It is speech not connected with the goal, Master Gotama.
“Indeed, young man, there are these five hindrances.”
Which five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt—
these, young man, are the five hindrances.
"By these five hindrances, young man, the brahmin Pokkharasāti is obstructed, shut in, enveloped, and hemmed in by Subhaga-vanika Opamañña.
That he should know or see or realize any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—that is impossible.
These, young man, are the five strands of sensual pleasure."
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear … [and so on] … [as above].
Odors cognizable by the nose...
tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust—
"These, young man, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.

Now, young man, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, together with Opamañña and Subhagavanika, enjoys these five cords of sensual pleasure, being bound by them, infatuated with them, and utterly absorbed in them;
he does not see the danger in them and lacks the wisdom for their escape. That he should know or see or realize any superhuman state, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision—that is impossible."
“What do you think, young man:
would a fire burn by means of a supply of grass and wood, or would a fire burn without a supply of grass and wood? Which of these fires would have flames, color, and radiance?
“If, Master Gotama, that place were able to kindle a fire without a supply of grass and wood, then that fire would indeed have flames, color, and radiance.”
“It is impossible, young man, it cannot happen, that a fire could burn without having abandoned its fuel of grass and wood, except by means of psychic power.
Just as, young man, a fire burns dependent on a supply of grass and wood, even so, young man, I say this rapture is dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Just as, young man, a fire burns having abandoned its supply of grass and wood, even so, young man, I say this rapture is apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states.”
And what, young man, is rapture apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states?
Here, young man, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
This too, young man, is rapture apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.
Furthermore, student, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna.
This rapture, student, is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.
Those brahmins, student, who prescribe five things for the performance of merit, for the accomplishment of the wholesome—
“What, Master Gotama, do the brahmins prescribe here as the quality that bears greater fruit for the performance of merit and the accomplishment of the wholesome?
“Those five qualities which these brahmins prescribe for the performance of merit and the accomplishment of the wholesome— among them, Master Gotama,
the brahmins prescribe generosity as the quality that bears greater fruit for the performance of merit and the accomplishment of the wholesome.”
“What do you think, student?
Suppose a certain brahmin here were to have a great sacrifice prepared.
Then two brahmins might come along:”
‘We shall partake in the great sacrifice of the brahmin so-and-so.
Then, it might occur to one brahmin:

‘Oh, may I alone receive the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost alms-food in the dining hall; may no other brahmin receive the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost alms-food in the dining hall.’

"It is indeed possible, young man, that another brahmin might receive the seat of honor, the water of honor, and the alms-food of honor at the meal hall, while that brahmin does not receive the seat of honor, the water of honor,

and the alms-food of honor at the meal hall. Thinking, 'Another brahmin receives the seat of honor, the water of honor, and the alms-food of honor at the meal hall, but I do not receive the seat of honor, the water of honor,
and the alms-food of honor,' he becomes angry and displeased."
“But what, young man, do the brahmins prescribe as the result of this?
“In this matter, Master Gotama, the brahmins do not give gifts with the thought:
‘By this may another be angry and displeased.’”
“But in this case, young man, the brahmins give gifts that are merely of the nature of compassion.
“That being so, young man, this is the sixth basis for making merit for the brahmins:
namely, that which is of the nature of compassion.”
“If this is so, Master Gotama, this is the sixth basis for making merit for the brahmins,
namely, ‘being born out of compassion. “Student,
as for those five things that the brahmins prescribe for the performance of merit, for the accomplishment of the wholesome— where do you see these five things most frequently?”
“Is it among householders or among those who have gone forth?

“Sir Gotama, as for these five things that these brahmins prescribe for the performance of merit, for the accomplishment of what is wholesome—I observe these five things mostly among those who have gone forth and only rarely among householders.
For a householder, sir Gotama, has great responsibilities, great duties, great burdens, and great undertakings; he does not speak truthfully at all times and continuously.”
But one who has gone forth, Master Gotama, has few concerns, few duties, few responsibilities, and little exertion; he is constantly and continuously a speaker of truth.
For a householder, Master Gotama, has many concerns, many duties, many responsibilities, and great exertion; he is not constantly and continuously an ascetic...
nor does he live the holy life...
He is devoted to recitation… he is devoted to generosity;
moreover, O Gotama, one who has gone forth has few concerns, few duties, few legal matters, and little exertion, and is constantly and continuously ascetic.
He is one who leads the holy life;
he is one who is abundant in recitation;
he is one who is abundant in generosity.

“Master Gotama, the brahmins prescribe five things for the performance of merit, for the accomplishment of what is wholesome. I observe these five things frequently among those who have gone forth, but rarely among householders.

“Māṇava, regarding those five things which the brahmins prescribe for the performance of merit, for the accomplishment of what is wholesome, I call them requisites of the mind—that is, the mind that is free from enmity and free from affliction, and the cultivation thereof.”
In this case, student, a bhikkhu is a speaker of truth.
Thinking, “I am a speaker of truth,” he gains knowledge of the meaning, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma.
That joy connected with the wholesome, I say, is an equipment for the mind.
That is to say, for the cultivation of a mind that is free from enmity and free from affliction.
Here, student, a bhikkhu is an ascetic … [as before] … he is a practitioner of celibacy … [as before].
He is devoted to recitation...
he is devoted to generosity.
Thinking, "I am devoted to generosity," he gains knowledge of the meaning, he gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and he gains joy connected with the Dhamma.
That joy connected with the wholesome, I call an equipment for the mind— that is,
for the cultivation of a mind that is free from enmity and free from affliction.
Those five things, student, which the brahmins prescribe for the performance of merit and for the attainment of the wholesome, I call equipment for the mind.
"That is to say, the cultivation of a mind that is free from enmity and free from ill will.
When this was said, the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, said this to the Blessed One:
"I have heard this, Master Gotama:..."
‘The ascetic Gotama knows the path to the company of Brahmā.
[The Buddha said: “What do you think, young man?
Is the village of Naḷakāra near here, or is the village of Naḷakāra far from here?”
“Yes, sir, the village of Naḷakāra is near here; the village of Naḷakāra is not far from here.

“What do you think, young man? Suppose there were a man born and raised in the village of Naḷakāra, and as soon as he had arrived back there from the village of Naḷakāra, people were to ask him the way to the village of Naḷakāra.”
“Māṇava, would there perhaps be any hesitation or delay for that man, born and raised in Naḷakāragāma, when asked the way to Naḷakāragāma?
“No indeed, Master Gotama. “And why is that?”
“Indeed, Master Gotama, that man was born and raised in Naḷakāra Village; all the roads to Naḷakāra Village are well known to him.
“Might there be, young man, for that man born and raised in Naḷakāra Village, any hesitation or delay when asked about the road to Naḷakāra Village?
But surely there would be none for the Tathāgata regarding the Brahmā-world?”
or hesitation or delay when asked about the way leading to the world of Brahmā.
For I, young man, understand Brahmā, the world of Brahmā, and the way leading to the world of Brahmā; and I also understand how one who has practiced accordingly is reborn in the world of Brahmā.
“I have heard this, Master Gotama:”
“The ascetic Gotama teaches the path to companionship with Brahmā.
“It would be well if the venerable Gotama would teach me the path to companionship with Brahmā.
“In that case, young man, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.”
“Yes, sir,” the young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, young brahmin, is the path to companionship with Brahmā?”
In this case, student, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,
likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself,
he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity.
He dwells pervading [the world] with a mind free from ill will.
Young man, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed in this way, whatever action is limited does not remain there, nor does it persist there.
Just as, young man, a powerful conch-blower can easily make himself heard in all four directions;

"In the same way, young man... [as before] ...When the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed in this way, young man, whatever action is limited will neither remain there nor persist there.
This, young man, is the path to the company of Brahmā.
"Furthermore, young man, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind imbued with compassion... [as before] ..."
With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy …pe… he dwells pervading one quarter with a mind accompanied by equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third,
likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, in every way, the entire world, he dwells pervading with a mind accompanied by equanimity.
He dwells having pervaded the mind with a vast, exalted, immeasurable, benevolent, and unblemished mind.
When equanimity as liberation of the mind has been developed in this way, young man, whatever karma is limited does not remain there, nor does it persist there.
Just as, young man, a powerful conch-blower can easily make himself heard in all four directions;
“In the same way, young man... [as before] ...When equanimity as liberation of mind has been developed in this way, young man, whatever action is limited will neither remain there nor persist there.
This, young man, is the path to the company of the Brahmās.
When this was said, the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!

Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; [even so has this Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways].”
In this very way, the Venerable Gotama has proclaimed the Dhamma by means of many methods.
I go for refuge to the Venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Venerable Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
"Now, Master Gotama, it is time for us to go;
we have many duties and much to do.
"Then, young man, go at your own convenience," he said.
Then the young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Now at that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was driving out from Sāvatthī during the middle of the day in an all-white chariot drawn by mares.
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi saw the young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, coming from afar.
Having seen the young man Subha, the son of Todeyya, he said this to him:
"Well now, from where does the venerable Bhāradvāja come so soon after midday?
"Indeed, sir, I am coming from the presence of the ascetic Gotama."
“What do you think, Master Bhāradvāja, do you consider the discernment of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama to be that of a wise man?
“Who am I, sir, and who am I to know the discernment of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama?
Surely only someone like him could know the discernment of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama.”
“Master Bhāradvāja indeed praises the ascetic Gotama with lofty praise.
“Who am I, sir, that I should praise the ascetic Gotama?
That venerable Gotama is praised by those who are themselves praised; he is the best among gods and humans.”
"Venerable sir, these five things which these brahmins prescribe for the performance of merit and the attainment of the wholesome—
the recluse Gotama calls them requisites for the mind;
that is to say, the development of a mind that is free from enmity and free from affliction."

When this was said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī descended from his all-white chariot drawn by mares, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his hands in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One,
uttered this inspired exclamation: “It is a gain for King Pasenadi of Kosala, it is a great gain for King Pasenadi of Kosala, that the Tathāgata, the Arahant,
the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwells within his realm.”
The ninth discourse, the Subha Sutta, is finished.
